docs.title: Creating a New Component
docs.text:
To add a new component to the workspace:

  1. Create a new directory in packages/.
  2. Initialize a new Python package with its own pyproject.toml.
  3. Add the package to the root pyproject.toml workspace members (already configured for packages/*).
  4. Run uv sync to update the workspace.

docs.title: Adding a Package
docs.text:
To add a new AI component package to the workspace:

mkdir -p packages/my-new-component/src/my_new_component
touch packages/my-new-component/pyproject.toml
touch packages/my-new-component/src/my_new_component/__init__.py

Add a pyproject.toml to the new package:

[project]
name = "my-new-component"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "A new AI component"
dependencies = []

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

Then run:

uv sync

docs.title: AI Component Architecture
docs.text: This document describes the architecture of the AI component for the Welding Quality Detection Challenge (Renault industrial use case).

docs.title: Two architectures considered
docs.text:
This document presents two distinct architectural approaches for the AI component. Each lifecycle phase below (Operation / Training / Evaluation) presents the relevant diagram(s) for both when available.

Approach Status Core idea BASE CASE Project consensus — adopted baseline Pre-processing pipeline (HSL conversion, unblur, un-rotate, flip), clusterize to 6 welding types, routing to one CNN per welding type (C20, C33, C102), MLP-based predictor + ODD detector, multi-timescale online monitoring. Uses ERP metadata (timestamp, weld ID, criticality, material). OPTIMIZATION Alternative explored — not adopted 2-stage pipeline: (1) Weld Localizer (YOLOv5n) → bbox_weld; (2) MIL classifier on cropped image_ROI with frozen YOLOv5s-C3CA backbone, attention pooling, weakly-supervised defect localization. Quality measurements (blur, luminosity) on image_ROI only.

Convention — When "the architecture" is mentioned without further qualifier (here or in other deliverables), it refers to BASE CASE. Any deviation, refinement or alternative must be explicitly attributed to OPTIMIZATION (or to a named new approach).

The sections below detail each phase. Module-level explanations, design rationale (e.g. Decision: YOLOv5) and the Software Constituents table at the end of the document refer to the OPTIMIZATION approach.

docs.title: OPTIMIZATION — Pipeline overview
docs.text:
The OPTIMIZATION approach implements a 2-stage pipeline designed for weakly-supervised defect detection. Image-level labels (OK / KO) are the only supervision available — no defect bounding-box annotations exist, hence the choice of MIL (Multi-Instance Learning) for defect classification.

  1. Stage 1 — Weld Localization: a lightweight detector finds the welding seam in the input image and outputs a bounding box bbox_weld.
  2. ROI cropping: the image is cropped to bbox_weld, producing image_ROI.
  3. Quality measurements on ROI only: blur and luminosity are computed on image_ROI (not on the full image) so that environmental clutter — background metal parts, secondary welds, shop lighting — does not bias the measurements.
  4. Trustworthy modules (OOD detector, online monitoring) receive both the latent representation and features derived from bbox_weld (position, size, aspect ratio). Geometric drift in the bbox is itself a strong OOD signal (seam moved, occluded, partial framing).
  5. Stage 2 — MIL defect classification on ROI: patches are extracted from image_ROI only; a frozen backbone produces patch embeddings; an attention-based MIL aggregator yields the final OK / KO / UNKNOWN decision and, when KO, a localized bbox_defect derived from the attention map.

Reference libraries: YOLOv5 (detection + backbone), PUNCC (uncertainty), OODeel (OOD), SAM (Segment Anything — used offline to bootstrap weld pseudo-labels).

High-level data flow:

Step Input Module Output 1 image Weld Localizer (YOLOv5n) bbox_weld 2 image + bbox_weld ROI Cropper image_ROI 3 image_ROI Blur Measure / Luminosity Measure blur_ROI, luminosity_ROI 4 image_ROI MIL Bag Builder patches 5 patches Backbone YOLOv5s-C3CA (frozen) latent embeddings 6 latent MIL Aggregator (attention pooling) bag score + attention map 7 bag score Predictor + UQ + OOD OK / KO / UNKNOWN + scores 8 attention map Defect Localizer bbox_defect (if KO) 9 bbox_weld, blur_ROI, luminosity_ROI, OOD score Online Monitoring drift indicators

Module-by-module notes (OPTIMIZATION):

  • Preprocessor: minimal — resize to a canonical size and normalize pixel intensities. No quality measurement here (deferred to post-ROI).
  • Weld Localizer: YOLOv5n outputs the weld bbox. Trained offline (see Training section). Single forward pass, ~10 ms on GPU.
  • ROI Cropper: pure utility (cv2 + small padding). Adapts the canonical size of image_ROI to MIL bag builder constraints.
  • Blur / Luminosity Measure: computed on image_ROI only. The blur_level and luminosity_level fields in the dataset metadata correspond to full-image measurements; the monitoring values used here are the ROI-restricted versions.
  • MIL Bag Builder: extracts a fixed grid of patches (or sliding window with overlap) from image_ROI. Each patch becomes one MIL "instance".
  • Backbone: YOLOv5s-C3CA, frozen weights from ImageNet pre-training. Outputs a feature vector per patch.
  • MIL Aggregator: attention-based pooling (Ilse et al. 2018) that learns per-patch attention weights and aggregates instance embeddings into a bag-level embedding.
  • Predictor: classification head on the bag embedding → OK or KO. Returns UNKNOWN if the conformal prediction set (PUNCC) is empty or if the OOD score crosses a threshold.
  • UQ (PUNCC): conformal prediction calibrated offline — provides confidence sets with formal coverage guarantees.
  • OOD Detector (OODeel): receives both the latent representation and geometric features of bbox_weld (position, size, aspect ratio relative to per-(seam, resolution) reference). Geometric drift = early OOD signal.
  • Online Monitoring: aggregates blur_ROI, luminosity_ROI, bbox_weld features and OOD score into rolling-window indicators of operational drift.
  • Defect Localizer: when KO, picks the patch(es) with the highest MIL attention weight and projects their position back into image_ROI coordinates → bbox_defect. Weakly-supervised localization.

docs.title: Decision: YOLOv5 — still relevant? (OPTIMIZATION)
docs.text:
Applies to the OPTIMIZATION approach. The BASE CASE uses a different backbone strategy (one CNN per welding type, not specified as YOLOv5).

Verdict: yes, but with a clarified role on two distinct models.

docs.title: Stage 1 — Weld Localizer: YOLOv5n
docs.text:
• ~1.9M parameters, ~10 ms inference on a modern GPU. Fits the latency budget (median < 200 ms total per KPI Performance).
  • The welding seam is a well-delimited object on a contrasted background — a lightweight detector is sufficient; no need for transformer-class capacity.
  • Cameras have a fixed viewpoint per seam, so the bbox distribution is restricted → fast convergence, easy generalization.
  • Pseudo-labels are generated offline with SAM (no inference-time cost), then YOLOv5n is fine-tuned from ImageNet weights.

docs.title: Stage 2 — Defect Classification: YOLOv5s-C3CA backbone (frozen) + MIL head
docs.text:
• The C3CA blocks integrate Coordinate Attention, which preserves spatial information after pooling → useful for an attention-based MIL aggregator that needs to localize defects from patch importance.
  • The s variant is sufficient because the input is already cropped to image_ROI (smaller than the full image), reducing the parameter count needed.
  • YOLOv5 is not used in detection mode here: the dataset only provides image-level labels (OK / KO), so a supervised detector for defects is impossible. The MIL paradigm is the appropriate response to weak supervision.
  • Defect localization (bbox_defect) is done via the MIL attention map (Ilse et al. 2018), not via a YOLO head — no defect bbox supervision is available.

docs.title: Why not a different architecture?
docs.text:
• Vision Transformer + RoI pooling: more capacity but requires more data and inference time, both scarce. Overkill for a binary classification on ~22k images.
  • EfficientNet / ConvNeXt backbones: viable alternatives but lose the Coordinate Attention benefit; would be a candidate if YOLOv5s-C3CA shows poor MIL attention quality during evaluation.
  • End-to-end 1-stage detector (e.g. YOLOv5 trained on full image with weld + defect classes): impossible without defect bboxes.

docs.title: Software Constituents (OPTIMIZATION)
docs.text:
Applies to the OPTIMIZATION approach. The BASE CASE software constituents are illustrated by colour-coding inside its training diagram (software / real data / augmented data / training regime).

Module Implementation Role Preprocessor cv2 + numpy Resize to canonical size, normalize pixel intensities Weld Localizer YOLOv5n fine-tuned on SAM pseudo-labels image → bbox_weld ROI Cropper cv2 + padding utility image + bbox_weld → image_ROI Blur Measure cv2.Laplacian(image_ROI, CV_64F).var() → blur_ROI Luminosity Measure image_ROI.mean() (or HSV-V channel) → luminosity_ROI MIL Bag Builder grid or sliding window over image_ROI → patches Backbone YOLOv5s-C3CA (frozen, ImageNet pre-trained) patches → latent embeddings MIL Aggregator Attention pooling (Ilse et al. 2018) latent → bag embedding + attention map Predictor Classification head + UNKNOWN thresholding bag embedding → OK / KO / UNKNOWN Defect Localizer argmax on attention map + bbox projection attention map → bbox_defect (KO only) Uncertainty Quantifier PUNCC (conformal prediction) bag embedding → confidence set OOD Detector OODeel + geometric features of bbox_weld latent + bbox → OOD score Online Monitoring rolling-window aggregator blur_ROI, luminosity_ROI, bbox_weld, OOD score → drift indicators

docs.title: AI Component Architecture
docs.text: This document describes the architecture of the AI component for the Welding Quality Detection Challenge (Renault industrial use case).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The component implements a 2-stage pipeline designed for weakly-supervised defect detection. Image-level labels (OK / KO) are the only supervision available — no defect bounding-box annotations exist, hence the choice of MIL (Multi-Instance Learning) for defect classification.

  1. Stage 1 — Weld Localization: a lightweight detector finds the welding seam in the input image and outputs a bounding box bbox_weld.
  2. ROI cropping: the image is cropped to bbox_weld, producing image_ROI.
  3. Quality measurements on ROI only: blur and luminosity are computed on image_ROI (not on the full image) so that environmental clutter — background metal parts, secondary welds, shop lighting — does not bias the measurements.
  4. Trustworthy modules (OOD detector, online monitoring) receive both the latent representation and features derived from bbox_weld (position, size, aspect ratio). Geometric drift in the bbox is itself a strong OOD signal (seam moved, occluded, partial framing).
  5. Stage 2 — MIL defect classification on ROI: patches are extracted from image_ROI only; a frozen backbone produces patch embeddings; an attention-based MIL aggregator yields the final OK / KO / UNKNOWN decision and, when KO, a localized bbox_defect derived from the attention map.

Reference libraries: YOLOv5 (detection + backbone), PUNCC (uncertainty), OODeel (OOD), SAM (Segment Anything — used offline to bootstrap weld pseudo-labels).

Module-by-module notes:

  • Preprocessor: minimal — resize to a canonical size and normalize pixel intensities. No quality measurement here (deferred to post-ROI).
  • Weld Localizer: YOLOv5n outputs the weld bbox. Trained offline (see Training section). Single forward pass, ~10 ms on GPU.
  • ROI Cropper: pure utility (cv2 + small padding). Adapts the canonical size of image_ROI to MIL bag builder constraints.
  • Blur / Luminosity Measure: computed on image_ROI only. The blur_level and luminosity_level fields in the dataset metadata correspond to full-image measurements; the monitoring values used here are the ROI-restricted versions.
  • MIL Bag Builder: extracts a fixed grid of patches (or sliding window with overlap) from image_ROI. Each patch becomes one MIL "instance".
  • Backbone: YOLOv5s-C3CA, frozen weights from ImageNet pre-training. Outputs a feature vector per patch.
  • MIL Aggregator: attention-based pooling (Ilse et al. 2018) that learns per-patch attention weights and aggregates instance embeddings into a bag-level embedding.
  • Predictor: classification head on the bag embedding → OK or KO. Returns UNKNOWN if the conformal prediction set (PUNCC) is empty or if the OOD score crosses a threshold.
  • UQ (PUNCC): conformal prediction calibrated offline — provides confidence sets with formal coverage guarantees.
  • OOD Detector (OODeel): receives both the latent representation and geometric features of bbox_weld (position, size, aspect ratio relative to per-(seam, resolution) reference). Geometric drift = early OOD signal.
  • Online Monitoring: aggregates blur_ROI, luminosity_ROI, bbox_weld features and OOD score into rolling-window indicators of operational drift.
  • Defect Localizer: when KO, picks the patch(es) with the highest MIL attention weight and projects their position back into image_ROI coordinates → bbox_defect. Weakly-supervised localization.

docs.title: Decision: YOLOv5 — still relevant?
docs.text: Verdict: yes, but with a clarified role on two distinct models.

docs.title: Stage 1 — Weld Localizer: YOLOv5n
docs.text:
• ~1.9M parameters, ~10 ms inference on a modern GPU. Fits the latency budget (median < 200 ms total per KPI Performance).
  • The welding seam is a well-delimited object on a contrasted background — a lightweight detector is sufficient; no need for transformer-class capacity.
  • Cameras have a fixed viewpoint per seam, so the bbox distribution is restricted → fast convergence, easy generalization.
  • Pseudo-labels are generated offline with SAM (no inference-time cost), then YOLOv5n is fine-tuned from ImageNet weights.

docs.title: Stage 2 — Defect Classification: YOLOv5s-C3CA backbone (frozen) + MIL head
docs.text:
• The C3CA blocks integrate Coordinate Attention, which preserves spatial information after pooling → useful for an attention-based MIL aggregator that needs to localize defects from patch importance.
  • The s variant is sufficient because the input is already cropped to image_ROI (smaller than the full image), reducing the parameter count needed.
  • YOLOv5 is not used in detection mode here: the dataset only provides image-level labels (OK / KO), so a supervised detector for defects is impossible. The MIL paradigm is the appropriate response to weak supervision.
  • Defect localization (bbox_defect) is done via the MIL attention map (Ilse et al. 2018), not via a YOLO head — no defect bbox supervision is available.

docs.title: Why not a different architecture?
docs.text:
• Vision Transformer + RoI pooling: more capacity but requires more data and inference time, both scarce. Overkill for a binary classification on ~22k images.
  • EfficientNet / ConvNeXt backbones: viable alternatives but lose the Coordinate Attention benefit; would be a candidate if YOLOv5s-C3CA shows poor MIL attention quality during evaluation.
  • End-to-end 1-stage detector (e.g. YOLOv5 trained on full image with weld + defect classes): impossible without defect bboxes.

docs.text: Module Implementation Role Preprocessor cv2 + numpy Resize to canonical size, normalize pixel intensities Weld Localizer YOLOv5n fine-tuned on SAM pseudo-labels image → bbox_weld ROI Cropper cv2 + padding utility image + bbox_weld → image_ROI Blur Measure cv2.Laplacian(image_ROI, CV_64F).var() → blur_ROI Luminosity Measure image_ROI.mean() (or HSV-V channel) → luminosity_ROI MIL Bag Builder grid or sliding window over image_ROI → patches Backbone YOLOv5s-C3CA (frozen, ImageNet pre-trained) patches → latent embeddings MIL Aggregator Attention pooling (Ilse et al. 2018) latent → bag embedding + attention map Predictor Classification head + UNKNOWN thresholding bag embedding → OK / KO / UNKNOWN Defect Localizer argmax on attention map + bbox projection attention map → bbox_defect (KO only) Uncertainty Quantifier PUNCC (conformal prediction) bag embedding → confidence set OOD Detector OODeel + geometric features of bbox_weld latent + bbox → OOD score Online Monitoring rolling-window aggregator blur_ROI, luminosity_ROI, bbox_weld, OOD score → drift indicators

docs.title: 1.1 Operator (Production Line - OP 120)
docs.text:
As an operations centered developement we shall consider first the point of view of the operator. As the primary human responsible of the weld defaults detection and main user of the AI component, the operator has the folowwing requirements:

  • Visualization of:
    • the various weld images:
      • the weld ID
      • the weld type
      • the localization of the weld defaults if any
    • the prediction result:
      • OK / KO / UNKNOWN status
      • confidence score
  • Selection & Validation:
    • Selection (by finger touch) of the OK images (= weld without defaults)
    • Validation of the selected images (= OK images)
  • Visualization of the following metrics:
    • Latency vs acceptance limit
    • the actual percentages of OK, KO & UNKNOWN vs allowable limits
    • the OOD detector metrics for each type of weld:
      • measured luminosity vs ODD range
      • blur level vs ODD range
      • rotation vs ODD range
      • weld position vs ODD range
  • Raise of Warning / Alarm in case the following events occur:
    • AI component issues:
      • Latency gets over allowable limit (something may have to be fixed on the AI component working conditions)
    • Production line issues:
      • percentage of KO or UNKNOWN gets over allowable limits for a certain weld type
      • an ODD related metric gets OOD

KPIs used: confidence scores, OOD score, Unknown rate (batch) Aggregation method: per-image display (no aggregation), batch summary uses simple counts and moving averages Phase: Operation only

docs.title: 1.2 Product Owner
docs.text:
The Product Owner (PO) is the ultimate responsable of the AI component in all its aspects and all its phases (development, training, validation, operation, maintenance). As such he is part of the audience of any artefact created in the project. In addition to artefacts mainly dedicated to other stakeholders, the PO should have its own specific dashboards that allows her/him to have an overview on the overall performance and level thrustworthiness of its AI component. We would typically consider a specific dashboard for each single phase as follows:

  • Artefact: Trust synthesis report for deployment go/no-go decision.
  • Content:
  • Radar chart of the 6 trust attributes (performance, uncertainty, robustness, OOD, generalization, data drift) — immediate visual overview
  • Pass/fail status per attribute against defined thresholds
  • Weighted global trust score for cross-version comparison
  • Go/no-go recommendation
  • KPIs used: all 13 KPIs aggregated into trust attributes
  • Aggregation method: two-level approach — (1) pass/fail gate: each attribute must meet its minimum threshold, (2) weighted score: normalized KPIs combined with criticality-based weights (Performance ×3, OOD ×2, Robustness ×2, Uncertainty ×1, Generalization ×1, Drift ×1)
  • Phase: Evaluation

docs.title: 1.3 Quality & Safety Officer
docs.text:
• Artefact: Compliance and reliability report.

  • Confusion matrix per seam type (C20/C33/C102) — detailed error analysis
  • Operational cost matrix — false negative impact weighted by weld criticality
  • Robustness report: ΔF1-score per perturbation type with ODD compliance assessment
  • OOD detection reliability: AUROC OOD, false negative OOD rate
  • Data drift behavior: performance stability curve under increasing degradation
  • Operator correction patterns and missed defect estimates
  • KPIs used: Performance, Robustness, OOD Monitoring, Data Drift, Sampling Rules Efficiency
  • Aggregation method: per seam type breakdown, per perturbation type breakdown, criticality weighting for cost matrix
  • Phase: Evaluation, Operation

docs.title: 1.4 Technical Team (Data Scientists / ML Engineers)
docs.text:
• Artefact: Detailed technical report for model improvement and production monitoring.
  • Content:
  • During development: training loss curves, F1-score evolution per epoch, train/val gap (overfitting detection), data quality metrics (class distribution, annotation consistency, ODD coverage)
  • During evaluation: detailed confusion matrices, ECE and Brier score analysis, per-class and per-seam performance breakdown, robustness curves per perturbation type and intensity level, generalization performance on unseen seams (C19/C34/C101)
  • During operation: real-time monitoring dashboard — confidence score distribution, Unknown rate trends, OOD detection frequency, drift indicators, latency tracking, operator feedback log

docs.title: Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)
docs.text: This document defines the KPIs used to measure the performance and trustworthiness of the AI component for the Welding Quality Detection Challenge. KPIs are organized around the 6 trust attributes defined in the Confiance.ai evaluation framework, plus component-specific KPIs tied to the specialized architecture (routing, per-CNN performance, preprocessing correction, sampling rules).

docs.title: 1. Data Quality KPI
docs.text:
• Description: Evaluate the quality and representativeness of the dataset before training begins, ensuring sufficient coverage of the operational design domain.
  • Metrics:
  • Class distribution: ratio OK/KO per seam type (C20/C33/C102). Detect severe imbalance or missing defect samples for a specific seam.
  • Annotation consistency: agreement rate between operator and quality controller annotations. Low agreement signals labeling noise that could harm training.
  • ODD coverage: diversity of capture conditions represented in the dataset (lighting variations, blur levels, rotation angles). Gaps in coverage indicate blind spots.
  • Objective: All seam types represented with both OK and KO samples, annotation consistency > threshold (TBD), ODD conditions sufficiently covered.
  • Phase: Construction.

docs.title: 2. Training Convergence KPI
docs.text:
• Description: Monitor the progression and stability of model training to detect issues early (divergence, overfitting, instability).
  • Metrics:
  • Loss evolution: training loss should decrease smoothly without oscillation.
  • F1-score on validation set per epoch: tracks model improvement over time.
  • Train/val gap: difference between training F1 and validation F1. A growing gap signals overfitting (model memorizes training data instead of learning generalizable features).
  • Objective: Smooth convergence, F1 val plateau triggers early stopping, train/val gap < threshold (TBD).
  • Phase: Training.

docs.title: 3. Performance KPI
docs.text:
• Description: Evaluate the component's ability to correctly classify welds, prioritizing defect detection (minimizing false negatives is the top priority — a defective weld classified as OK is a safety risk).
  • Metrics:
  • Recall NOK: proportion of actual defects correctly detected. Recall = TP / (TP + FN). A recall of 0.95 means the model misses 5% of defects.
  • Precision NOK: when the model predicts NOK, is it correct? Precision = TP / (TP + FP). Low precision means too many false alarms.
  • F1-score: harmonic mean of precision and recall (global + per class + per seam type). A single indicator balancing both.
  • Confusion matrix: cross-tabulation of predictions vs true classes (OK/NOK/Unknown), broken down by seam type (C20/C33/C102) to identify seam-specific weaknesses.
  • Operational cost matrix: asymmetric cost weighting — a false negative (NOK classified as OK) costs significantly more than a false positive (OK classified as NOK), especially on critical welds.
  • Inference latency: time from image input to prediction output. Must remain under 1/12s (~83ms).
  • Objective: Recall NOK > threshold (TBD), F1 NOK > threshold (TBD), inference latency < 1/12s.
  • Phase: Evaluation, Operation.

docs.title: 4. Uncertainty KPI
docs.text:
• Description: Evaluate the relevance and calibration of the component's confidence estimates, ensuring alignment between expressed uncertainty and actual error risk. A model that displays 90% confidence should be correct ~90% of the time.
  • Metrics:
  • ECE (Expected Calibration Error): measures the gap between expressed confidence and actual accuracy, grouped by confidence bins. An ECE of 0.05 means confidence is off by 5% on average.
  • Brier Score: global measure of predicted probability quality, combining calibration and discrimination. Ranges from 0 (perfect) to 1 (worst).
  • Unknown rate: percentage of predictions routed to Unknown. Must be within a target range — too high means the model is useless, too low means it may miss doubtful cases.
  • Objective: ECE < threshold (TBD), Unknown rate within target range (e.g. 2-10%).
  • Phase: Evaluation, Operation.

docs.title: 5. Robustness KPI
docs.text:
• Description: Evaluate the component's ability to produce stable predictions under ODD-compliant perturbations (blur, lighting, rotation ±10°, translation ~20px).
  • Metrics:
  • ΔF1-score under perturbation: difference in F1-score between clean images and perturbed images, per perturbation type. Smaller delta = more robust.
  • AUC of precision per perturbation level: F1-score curve as perturbation intensity increases. Area under this curve gives a global robustness score. A robust model maintains a flat curve.
  • Unknown switch rate under perturbation: does the Unknown rate increase reasonably under perturbation? If it explodes → model too sensitive. If it doesn't move → model may not detect it's struggling.
  • Objective: ΔF1 < acceptable threshold (e.g. < 5% degradation), stable behavior within ODD limits.
  • Phase: Evaluation.

docs.title: 6. OOD Monitoring KPI
docs.text:
• Description: Evaluate the component's ability to detect out-of-distribution inputs (dirty camera, saturated image, unknown object, extreme blur) and flag them as Unknown rather than producing unreliable predictions.
  • Metrics:
  • AUROC OOD: global ability to separate in-distribution from OOD images. Ranges from 0.5 (random) to 1.0 (perfect separation).
  • OOD false negative rate: OOD image not detected → passes through the model with potentially meaningless prediction. Most dangerous case, to be minimized.
  • OOD false positive rate: normal image flagged as OOD → unnecessary Unknown, overloads operator with manual checks.
  • Objective: AUROC OOD > threshold (e.g. > 0.95), OOD false negative rate minimized.
  • Phase: Evaluation, Operation.

docs.title: 7. Generalization KPI
docs.text:
• Description: Evaluate the component's ability to classify unseen weld seam types (C19, C34, C101) that share visual features with training data, without retraining.
  • Metrics:
  • F1-score on unseen seams: same metric as performance KPI, computed on unseen seam types.
  • ΔF1 seen vs unseen: performance gap between training seam types and unseen ones. Small delta = good generalization.
  • Confusion matrix on unseen seams: to check whether error patterns on unseen seams differ from seen seams.
  • Unknown rate on unseen seams: is the model appropriately less confident on new seam types? A slightly higher Unknown rate would indicate healthy caution.
  • Objective: Acceptable performance on unseen seam types without retraining, ΔF1 < threshold.
  • Phase: Evaluation.

docs.title: 8. Data Drift KPI
docs.text:
• Description: Evaluate the component's ability to handle progressive hardware degradation: maintain performance under mild drift, and trigger OOD detection under severe drift.
  • Metrics:
  • F1-score per degradation level: performance at each intensity level (mild → moderate → severe Gaussian noise, dead pixels). Shows at which point the model breaks down.
  • OOD trigger point: at which degradation level does the OOD detector start firing? Too early → too sensitive. Too late → model predicts poorly without signaling it.
  • AUROC OOD under severe drift: does OOD detection work specifically on hardware-degraded images?
  • False negative rate under drift: degraded image neither detected as OOD nor correctly classified — model says OK on an unusable image. Most dangerous case.
  • Objective: Stable performance under mild drift, reliable OOD detection under severe drift.
  • Phase: Evaluation, Operation.

docs.title: 9. Routing Accuracy KPI
docs.text:
• Description: Evaluate whether the clusterizer correctly routes images to the appropriate specialized CNN. A misrouted image (e.g. C20 image sent to CNN C33) will produce unreliable predictions.
  • Metrics:
  • Routing accuracy: percentage of images correctly assigned to their corresponding CNN.
  • Routing confusion matrix: cross-tabulation of true seam types vs assigned CNN, to identify systematic misrouting patterns.
  • Objective: Routing accuracy > threshold (TBD), no systematic misrouting between seam types.
  • Phase: Evaluation.

docs.title: 10. Blur Detection Quality KPI
docs.text:
• Description: Evaluate the reliability of the blur analysis module (blur level → blur class). Incorrect blur classification can trigger unnecessary unblurring (degrading image quality) or miss blur that should have been corrected, and can also corrupt the blur-related OOD signal.
  • Metrics:
  • Blur classification accuracy: agreement between predicted blur class and ground truth blur level.
  • Impact on downstream performance: ΔF1-score with correct vs incorrect blur classification.
  • Objective: Blur classification accuracy > threshold (TBD), minimal impact on downstream prediction quality.
  • Phase: Evaluation.

docs.title: 11. Per-CNN Performance KPI
docs.text:
• Description: Evaluate the performance of each specialized CNN independently. Since each CNN is trained on its own seam type, individual degradation could go unnoticed if only global performance is tracked.
  • Metrics:
  • F1-score per CNN: F1 on OK/NOK classification for CNN C20, CNN C33, CNN C102 independently.
  • Recall NOK per CNN: false negative rate per specialized CNN.
  • Cross-CNN performance gap: max performance difference between the best and worst performing CNN. A large gap indicates imbalanced training quality.
  • Objective: All CNNs above minimum F1 threshold, cross-CNN gap < acceptable limit.
  • Phase: Evaluation, Operation.

docs.title: 12. Preprocessing Correction Quality KPI
docs.text:
• Description: Evaluate whether the unblur and un-rotate modules (trained with augmented data) actually improve image quality and downstream prediction performance, rather than introducing artifacts.
  • Metrics:
  • ΔF1 with/without correction: performance difference when preprocessing corrections are applied vs bypassed.
  • Image quality score before/after: objective image quality metric (e.g. sharpness, SSIM) before and after correction.
  • Objective: Corrections should improve or maintain downstream F1-score. If corrections degrade performance, they should be bypassed.
  • Phase: Evaluation.

docs.title: 13. Sampling Rules Efficiency KPI
docs.text:
• Description: Evaluate whether the sampling rules that select which predictions are shown to the operator are effective — catching the right cases for human review without overwhelming the operator.
  • Metrics:
  • Operator correction rate on sampled images: how often does the operator override the system's prediction on sampled images?
  • Missed defect rate on non-sampled images: estimated rate of undetected defects among images not shown to the operator (measurable via batch control).
  • Operator workload: number of images requiring manual review per shift.
  • Objective: High correction capture rate, low missed defect rate, manageable operator workload.
  • Phase: Operation.

docs.title: Aggregation Method
docs.text:
KPIs are aggregated using a two-level approach: 1. Pass/fail gate: each KPI must meet its minimum threshold — any failure blocks deployment 2. Weighted score: KPIs are normalized (0-1) and combined with criticality-based weights (e.g. Performance ×3, OOD ×2, Robustness ×2, Uncertainty ×1, Generalization ×1, Drift ×1) for cross-version comparison and progress tracking

docs.title: Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)
docs.text:
This document defines the KPIs used to assess the performance and trustworthiness of the AI component, and the methodology to aggregate them into a single trust score.

The methodology follows a multi-criteria aggregation pipeline, structured around 5 trust attributes covered here:

  1. Performance — predictive accuracy and operational cost
  2. Uncertainty — quality of confidence estimates
  3. Robustness — invariance to perturbations within the ODD
  4. OOD Monitoring — ability to flag inputs outside the ODD
  5. Generalization — stability across unseen weld types

A 6th attribute, Data-Drift handling, is documented in the original challenge protocol but is deferred for this iteration of the TP — see § Deferred: Data-Drift handling.

docs.title: KPI Mapping to Lifecycle Phases
docs.text: Trust attribute Construction Training Evaluation Operation Performance X X Uncertainty X X Robustness X X OOD Monitoring X X Generalization X Data-Drift (deferred) X

docs.title: 1. Performance
docs.text:
Purpose: Measure the model's predictive accuracy and efficiency, ensuring it meets baseline expectations in a controlled setting.

Evaluation set: Standard ML evaluation set — representative 20% split of the dataset.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
• OP-Perf (Operational Performance): confusion-matrix-based metric weighted by a non-symmetric cost matrix that penalizes errors according to weld criticality.
OP = Σ_k Σ_i Σ_j 𝟙{Top_class(ŷ_k) = j} · cost(i, j, k, k_seam)

Per-seam weights:

Seam k_seam c102 0.2 c20 0.4 c33 0.4

Cost matrix (asymmetric — false negatives heavily penalized):

Predicted KO Predicted OK Predicted UNKNOWN True KO 26.4 3000 41 True OK 30 0.4 20
  • ML-Perf: standard ML metric (precision / FBeta with β=1 since June 13).
ML = Σ 𝟙(y=1 ∧ ŷ=1) / Σ 𝟙(ŷ=1)
  • Times: 95th-percentile inference time on the evaluation set.

docs.title: Performance KPI
docs.text:
Combines OP and ML penalized by inference time:

I_perf = (α_op · exp(-k_c · OP) + α_ml · ML) / (1 + k_t · ln(1 + t))

Coefficients: α_op = 0.4, α_ml = 0.6, k_c = 1, k_t = 12.

docs.title: 2. Uncertainty
docs.text:
Purpose: Evaluate the AI component's ability to express calibrated uncertainty, helping operators assess decision risk.

Evaluation set: Standard ML evaluation set (20% split).

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
• U-OP (Uncertainty Operational Gain): relative virtual gain when using probabilistic outputs vs hard predictions.
c^U = Σ_k Σ_i Σ_j ŷ_k(j) · cost(i, j, k, k_seam)
UOP = (c^op - c^U) / (c^op - c^op_perfect)
  • U-Calib (Calibration Error): Expected Calibration Error, computed separately on OK and KO subsets to handle class imbalance.
UCalib = Σ_m (|B_m|/N) · |acc(B_m) - conf(B_m)|

Class weights: UCalib_OK = 0.2, UCalib_KO = 0.8.

docs.title: Uncertainty KPI
docs.text: I_U = UOP · (1 - 2 · (UCalib_KO · 0.2 + UCalib_OK · 0.8))

docs.title: 3. Robustness
docs.text:
Purpose: Assess model stability under perturbations within the ODD — blur, luminance, rotation, translation. Output should remain invariant as long as perturbations stay inside ODD bounds.

Evaluation set: Synthetic perturbations applied to a weld-balanced subset of the standard evaluation set, sweeping increasing perturbation levels.

docs.title: Perturbation ranges
docs.text: Perturbation Range explored Reference Rotation [-30°, +30°] (full ODD) — stress-tested in [-10°, +10°] Project ODD definition Translation (x, x) with x ∈ [0, 20] pixels (same bound for 1920×1080 and 960×540) evaluation_page.md:177 Blur Increasing intensity, upper bound set visually (weld no longer visible) evaluation_page.md:179 Luminance Increasing and decreasing intensity, bounds set visually evaluation_page.md:181

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
For each perturbation x ∈ {blur, lum, rot, trans}, the AUC of the ML-performance (precision / FBeta) is computed across perturbation levels:

r^x = AUC( ML_δ1, ML_δ2, ..., ML_δk )

docs.title: Robustness KPI
docs.text:
Weighted aggregation across the 4 perturbation types:

I_rob = α_blur · r^blur + α_lum · r^lum + α_rot · r^rot + α_trans · r^trans

Coefficients: α_blur = 0.3, α_lum = 0.3, α_rot = 0.2, α_trans = 0.2.

docs.title: 4. OOD Monitoring
docs.text:
Purpose: Evaluate the model's ability to detect inputs outside the ODD in an unsupervised way — primarily based on the criterion "is the weld sufficiently visible?". The component should return UNKNOWN for OOD inputs.

Evaluation sets: Two complementary OOD datasets, each balanced with normal samples.

  • OOD_real — built by manual inspection of real images: excessive blur, extreme lighting, visual obstructions hiding the weld.
  • OOD_syn — built by applying strong synthetic perturbations: heavy blur, abnormal luminance, severe color artifacts, Gaussian noise + dead pixels.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
• OOD_real: AUROC on the real OOD evaluation set.
  • OOD_syn: AUROC on the synthetic OOD evaluation set.

docs.title: OOD-Monitoring KPI
docs.text:
I_ood = α_syn · OOD_syn + α_real · OOD_real

Coefficients: α_syn = 0.3, α_real = 0.7 — real OOD weighted higher because it reflects production conditions.

docs.title: 5. Generalization
docs.text:
Purpose: Measure the model's ability to generalize to unseen weld types (C19, C34, C101) that share visual/structural traits with the training seams (c20, c33, c102).

Evaluation set: Built from welds excluded during training but with similar features.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
• OP_g: Operational performance on the generalization set (same OP formula and cost matrix as Performance).
  • ML_g: ML performance (precision / FBeta) on the generalization set.

docs.title: Generalization KPI
docs.text:
I_gen = α_op · exp(-k_op · OP_g) + α_ml · ML_g

Coefficients: k_op = 0.05, α_op = 0.4, α_ml = 0.6 (same α weights as the Performance attribute).

docs.title: Deferred: Data-Drift handling
docs.text:
The Data-Drift handling attribute (I_drift) is part of the original challenge evaluation protocol but is deferred for this iteration of the TP.

For reference, the protocol expects:

  • An operational drift dataset built by applying gradually increasing perturbations to a normal data sequence, with final segments manually labeled as OOD.
  • Two metrics: OP_d (operational performance under drift) and OOD_d (AUROC on the drift-induced OOD subset).
  • KPI formula: I_drift = α_OP · exp(-k_op · OP_d) + α_OOD · OOD_d with α_OP = α_OOD = 0.5, k_op = 0.05.
  • Aggregation weight in the global score: α_6 = 0.05 (lowest among attributes).

Why deferred: defining a representative drift sequence requires production telemetry over time, which is not in scope for this TP iteration. To be added once an operational data feed exists.

docs.title: Aggregation Methodology
docs.text: The 5 attribute KPIs above are aggregated into a single trust score using a 6-step pipeline. Notation: α_i, β_i, k_i are weighting / scaling coefficients.

docs.title: Step 1 — Compute attribute-specific metrics
docs.text: Each attribute is measured by one or several criteria computed on its dedicated evaluation set (cf. sections 1-5).

docs.title: Step 2 — Normalize each metric to [0, 1]
docs.text:
All raw metrics are mapped to [0, 1] (1 = best). Transformations depend on metric nature:

  • Cost-based metrics (OP, OP_g): lower is better → exponential decay exp(-k · x).
  • Bounded metrics (ML, AUROC, calibration): already in [0, 1], optionally rescaled.
  • Time: hyperbolic penalty 1 / (1 + k · ln(1 + t)).

docs.title: Step 3 — Aggregate per attribute → Trust-KPI I_X
docs.text:
For each attribute X, an attribute-specific aggregation function combines its k normalized metrics into a single trust KPI:

I_X = agg( X_metric_1, X_metric_2, ..., X_metric_k )

The exact agg function is chosen per attribute (cf. formulas in sections 1-5):

Attribute Aggregation function Performance weighted sum of OP/ML, divided by time penalty Uncertainty UOP × (1 - 2·UCalib) Robustness weighted sum of 4 AUC scores OOD Monitoring weighted sum of 2 AUROC scores Generalization weighted sum of OP_g/ML_g (same shape as Performance)

docs.title: Step 4 — Piecewise linear rescaling
docs.text:
Each attribute KPI undergoes a piecewise linear rescaling to align scores with predefined performance and confidence thresholds (α_1, α_2, β_1, β_2):

            ⎧ (β_1 / α_1) · f(x),                                        if 0 ≤ f(x) < α_1
f'(x)  =    ⎨ ((β_2 - β_1) / (α_2 - α_1)) · (f(x) - α_1) + β_1,           if α_1 ≤ f(x) ≤ α_2
            ⎩ ((1 - β_2) / (1 - α_2)) · (f(x) - α_2) + β_2,               if α_2 < f(x) ≤ 1

Practical effect (calibrated on virtual reference solutions): - A poor solution (e.g. always predicting UNKNOWN) scores around 10 / 100. - A good solution (~3% error rate) scores around 90 / 100 on most attributes.

docs.title: Step 5 — Weighted aggregation → final score
docs.text:
The rescaled attribute KPIs are combined by a weighted mean into the global trust score:

score = α_1 · I_perf + α_2 · I_U + α_3 · I_rob + α_4 · I_ood + α_5 · I_gen + α_6 · I_drift
Attribute Weight Performance α_1 = 0.30 Uncertainty α_2 = 0.15 Robustness α_3 = 0.25 OOD Monitoring α_4 = 0.20 Generalization α_5 = 0.05 Data-Drift (deferred) α_6 = 0.05

Note: in this iteration, I_drift is not computed — its weight is either redistributed to other attributes or the score is reported on the remaining 0.95 mass (to be decided when the global pipeline is implemented).

docs.title: Step 6 — Purpose
docs.text:
The final score is a single comparable number capturing performance across all trust attributes, designed to:

  • rank competing solutions on a fair basis,
  • highlight which attribute drags the overall score down (via the per-attribute breakdown),
  • align with operational and confidence requirements through the piecewise rescaling.
